title: British Police Arrest Men Driving Toward U.S. Bomber Base In The U.K. With Suspected Explosives
content: Details continue to come in, but police in the United Kingdom have declared a “major incident” and ordered evacuations near RAF Fairford after the arrest of “several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act,” the Gloucestershire Constabulary stated . RAF Fairford is a major hub for U.S. military aircraft in the United Kingdom. It is a regular host of strategic assets, including bombers and U-2 spy planes. It also acts as a pit stop for other aircraft, including fighters, that are being ferried to and from the United States. Bomber strikes launched from Fairford were a central aspect of major U.S. combat operations against Iran earlier this year. “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident,” the Gloucestershire Constabulary also announced today in light of the incident. Emergency services in Fairford after a major incident has been declared, with armed police manning a cordon near the village of Whelford in Gloucestershire, near RAF Fairford, which is used by the United States Air Force (USAF). (Photo by Ben Birchall/PA Images via Getty Images) Ben Birchall – PA Images The evacuations were spurred by the arrests. “The Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles,” Gloucestershire Constabulary added. “The local residents are being evacuated to a nearby leisure center.” “A cordon is currently in place, but we’d like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained,” the law enforcement agency explained.

title: Laser Weapons Will Be Deployed At Cape Canaveral Spaceport To Take Down Drones
content: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is getting lasers that can zap drones intruding into its airspace. When installed, the new directed energy defense system will be part of a much larger effort to protect the spaceport against drone incursions, a spokesperson for Space Launch Delta 45 (SLD 45) told us. The idea is to ensure the safety of launches and to keep prying eyes away from an installation full of secrets about America’s military and commercial space efforts. Companies like SpaceX, United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin and Relativity Space use the installation for space launches. The base defense modernization effort comes as the Cape Canaveral region is inundated with drone incursions. There were hundreds last year. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, on May 29, 2026. (U.S. Space Force photo by Gwen Kurzen) Gwendolyn Kurzen “As the world’s premier spaceport continues to support an unprecedented launch tempo for national security and commercial missions, securing critical launch infrastructure from low-altitude aerial threats remains a top operational priority,” the spokesperson explained. “The ongoing security modernization integrates detection, tracking, and defensive capabilities to include directed energy systems. These will provide security forces with real-time situational awareness and the necessary tools to safeguard personnel, launch complexes, and national security payloads.” The spokesperson did not have a timeline for when the directed energy system will be operational.

title: Bunker Talk: Let’s Talk About All The Things We Did And Didn’t Cover This Week
content: Welcome to Bunker Talk. This is a weekend open discussion post for the best commenting crew on the net, in which we can chat about all the stuff that went on this week that we didn’t cover. We can also talk about the stuff we did or whatever else grabs your interest. In other words, it’s an off-topic thread. This week’s caption reads: BERLIN, GERMANY JUNE 16: Heavy iron doors between different rooms during a media event on June 16, 2026, at the former Cold War-era Pankstraße subway station, now used as a nuclear fallout shelter. Built in the 1970s, the bunker offers sleeping accommodations for 3,339 people, has independent water and electricity supplies, and is hermetically sealed off from the outside world by massive steel doors. The bunker will be open to the public as part of guided tours of Berlin’s underground. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has rekindled German authorities’ interest in providing nuclear fallout shelters in the event of war. (Photo: Carsten Koall/Getty Images) PRIME DIRECTIVES: If you want to talk politics, do so respectfully and know that there’s always somebody that isn’t going to agree with you. title: Blackbeard Hypersonic Missile Seen Flying On F/A-18 Super Hornet For The First Time
content: The U.S. Navy has given us the first look at Blackbeard hypersonic strike missiles under the wings of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets during actual flight testing. The Navy is hoping to have Blackbeard in at least limited service no later than 2028, giving its carrier air wings an all-new fast-flying standoff weapon, particularly for engaging enemy ships. The missile is also being designed to be relatively cheap and quick to manufacture. The Navy’s Office of the Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Aviation (PAE-A) has released a video montage of Blackbeard undergoing flight testing, seen in the social media post below. The service confirmed that it had at least begun test-loading the missiles onto F/A-18E/F Super Hornets in a presentation at the Tailhook Association’s annual convention last month. Now we know the program has moved ahead substantially from that point. Coming soon to a theater near you…BLACKBEARD! @USPACOM @CENTCOM @PAEAviation pic.twitter.com/KgBtIqdf8I — NAVAIR (@NAVAIRNews) September 25, 2026 The company behind Blackbeard, defense start-up Castelion, has received several multi-million-dollar contracts from the Navy just this year explicitly to support integration of the weapon onto the Super Hornet, as well as otherwise accelerating its development.

title: Latvia To Order Anduril’s Barracuda Cruise Missile For Long-Range Strike Capability
content: NATO member Latvia is moving toward acquiring Anduril Industries’ Barracuda family of long-range strike missiles, with Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs highlighting the effort during a visit to the U.S. defense technology company and a series of new defense-industry cooperation agreements involving Latvia. If the acquisition goes through, Latvia would be the first of the Baltic states to field a strike weapon in this category. “It was great to visit Anduril to meet with Palmer Luckey and to witness signing of memoranda of cooperation with MOD of Latvia and Origin Robotics,” Rinkēvičs said in a post on X. “Looking forward to complete acquisition of Barracuda long-range missiles and [Latvian-U.S.] defense industry cooperation.” It was great to visit @anduriltech to meet with @PalmerLuckey and to witness signing of memoranda of cooperation with MOD of Latvia and @OriginRobotics . Looking forward to complete acquisition of Baracuda longe range missiles and defense industry cooperation pic.twitter.com/JafnNy5RAe — Edgars Rinkēvičs (@edgarsrinkevics) September 25, 2026 The statement does not specify the precise Barracuda variant involved, the number of missiles Latvia intends to acquire, the expected delivery schedule, or the value of the prospective purchase. We have reached out to Anduril for more details. A likely candidate weapon is the Barracuda-500M, one member of Anduril’s family of autonomous, jet-powered cruise missiles, alongside the Barracuda-100M and -250M variants.

title: Marines Rushing To Equip Amphibious Combat Vehicles With New Anti-Drone Jammers
content: The U.S. Marine Corps is buying Anduril Pulsar-L electronic warfare jammers to meet an urgent operational need to better protect its 8×8 wheeled Amphibious Combat Vehicles (ACV) from drones. This is part of broader efforts the service is pursuing to boost the ACV’s defenses against uncrewed aerial attackers, as well as incoming anti-tank guided missiles and other threats . Drone threats are real now and have notably sidelined even the most advanced heavy armor in Ukraine. Marine Corps Systems Command (MARCORSYSCOM) announced it had awarded a sole-source deal to Anduril, valued at $15,711,445.50, for an unspecified number of Pulsar-Ls, yesterday. This follows a statement of intent the Command put out last month. Anduril first unveiled Pulsar-L , a lightweight addition to its larger Pulsar family of electronic warfare systems , in April 2025. The Marine Corps had 150 baseline personnel carrier variants of the ACV (or ACV-Ps), as well as 21 command-and-control ACV-C versions, in inventory as of April 2026. The default armament for ACV-P currently is just a single .50 caliber M2 machine gun in a remote weapon station on top of the hull. The service’s goal is to eventually acquire 389 ACV-Ps and 33 ACV-Cs, as well as 152 ACV-30s with new 30mm cannon-armed turrets and 34 ACV-R armored recovery vehicle variants. The ACV family has already supplanted the Marine Corps’ previous fleet of tracked Assault Amphibious Vehicles (AAV).

title: An SR-71 Blackbird Has Vanished (Updated)
content: Last week, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman cryptically teased plans for a new high- and fast-flying X-plane with a silhouette of an aircraft that immediately drew comparisons to the famed SR-71 Blackbird as a backdrop. In our report, we looked at what it could mean, including the possibility of reviving the SR-71, or at least using it to inform or even cobble together a new airframe. Now it turns out that an SR-71 that had been on display at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center for years is suspiciously missing. Steve Trimble, Aviation Week ‘s defense editor and friend of TWZ , was first to report the disappearance of the former NASA SR-71, also known by the tail number 844, at Armstrong. That facility is collocated with Edwards Air Force Base in California. Trimble’s piece says that satellite imagery shows the jet has not been seen since at least May 17. The aircraft in question, which originally carried the U.S. Air Force serial number 61-7980, was the last Blackbird produced and the last one to fly, taking to the skies for the final time in 1999. A satellite image taken in 2018 showing SR-71, tail number 844, on display outside of the Armstrong Flight Research Center in California. Google Earth “The current disposition of the aircraft is unclear, but Aviation Week sources suggest that the aircraft was moved into a hangar earlier this year for an inspection,” according to the story.

title: China Appears To Be Building A Mothership For Large Uncrewed Submarines
content: For the past six months or so, a curious-looking vessel with a very boxy superstructure has been taking shape at a shipyard in the Chinese city of Shanghai. A new satellite image lends credence to an earlier assessment that this is a mothership to support China’s growing fleets of ever-larger submersible drones , though it could also have other roles. TWZ obtained the image of the ship in question, which was taken on September 10, from Vantor . Since then, it has also received an overall coat of gray paint, pointing to future service with the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN). It is some 669 feet (204 meters) long and around 98 feet (30 meters) at its widest. In terms of basic length and width, the vessel being built now is very roughly comparable to China’s Type 071 amphibious warfare ship . However, it appears to be much taller overall than the Type 071. The full September 10, 2026, image of the ship in question. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Another more recent view of the ship showing its new gray paint job. Chinese internet via X The new ship has been under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipyard on Changxing Island in Shanghai since at least April. This yard produces a variety of naval vessels, including surface combatants and amphibious assault ships, as well as commercial designs. The September 10 image, which shows the ship from the stern, is interesting for a number of reasons. It notably confirms that the design not only has a well deck, but that it is sized around what looks to be a large cradle-like platform visible in the shot.

title: France Sending Forces To Help Defend Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Oil Facilities
content: France is sending military assistance to Saudi Arabia to protect the Yanbu oil facilities as the Kingdom battles the Iran-backed Houthi rebels of Yemen. The move comes amid growing concerns about the remaining flow of oil from the region, which France, as well as the rest of Europe, relies upon heavily. In a live television interview Thursday night Paris time, French President Emmanuel Macron said he was sending an unspecified number of troops and equipment to Saudi Arabia to protect the Yanbu energy hub, located on the Red Sea. “This is the agreement we have finalized ​with ⁠the Saudis,” Macron explained. “We are going to send ⁠military resources, that is to ​say, soldiers, radar systems and defense ⁠systems, to protect this site — ⁠not ​to get us involved in any conflicts, but to ⁠protect this site.” The French leader did not elaborate on the exact equipment he would send, how many troops, or when they would arrive. Nor did he address what would happen if French personnel were killed or injured or equipment damaged or destroyed. We have reached out to the French Embassy for further details. Based on his mention of radars and seeing that the threat to Saudi oil infrastructure is almost entirely from aerial attacks from drones and missiles, these will likely be air defense forces. Nous agissons pour protéger nos compatriotes des conséquences de la crise au Moyen-Orient. Objectifs : sécuriser les approvisionnements et faire baisser les prix à la pompe.

title: F-35 Canopy And Weapons-Bay Door Loss To China: Separating Fact From Fiction
content: Chinese authorities have reportedly taken possession of an F-35 cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door that were inexplicably diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the United States. The incident appears to have left physical components that incorporate aspects of the fighter’s low-observable design in the hands of a country that has spent years doing whatever it could to gain information on the aircraft and America’s stealth technology secrets in general. So, what does all this mean? Let’s put it in perspective. The parts in question were being shipped by UPS from Australia to the United States in late May, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg . The components from a Royal Australian Air Force F-35A were being sent to the United States for inspection and possible repair or disposal. A Royal Australian Air Force F-35A from 75 Squadron taxiing at RAAF Base Tindal, Northern Territory. Australian Defense Force F-35 sustainment procedures explicitly cover the movement of F-35 parts, including unserviceable components, through the program’s logistics network. The U.S. Air Force’s transportation guidance directs F-35 shipments outside the Defense Transportation System to follow approved Joint Program Office procedures. In other words, moving an unserviceable Australian F-35 component to the United States for inspection, repair, or disposition is consistent with the normal sustainment process. What is highly unusual is where this particular shipment ended up.

title: 5 arrested in suspected terror plot at UK base used by US Air Force
content: British authorities arrested five people early Sunday morning on suspicion of planning terrorist actions near a base used by the U.S. Air Force. The United Kingdom’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement that the incident started shortly before 1 a.m. local time Sunday, when police got a call about a trio of “suspicious vehicles” moving towards RAF Fairford in southwest England. Five suspects, who authorities have not yet identified, were arrested on suspicion of plotting terrorism and explosive actions. The exact nature and scale of the suspected attack was also not disclosed. Counterterrorism officers are leading the investigation and searching the vans. The Air Force has a major presence in the United Kingdom, and bases such as RAF Fairford, Lakenheath and Mildenhall have served as stopover points for bombers, transports and fighter jets deploying to the Middle East. Air Force B-52 Stratofortresses and B-1B Lancers operated out of RAF Fairford to conduct missions against Iran at the start of the Iran war this year. The Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing is based out of Fairford. In a statement to Task & Purpose, an Air Force spokesperson said that the “501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners. The safety and security of our airmen, families, and surrounding communities remains our highest priority. We remain in close coordination with our U.K.

title: Former Fort Hood soldier sentenced to nearly six years for hacking, extortion plot
content: A former soldier was sentenced to 70 months in prison last week for a spree of various cybercrimes spanning years, while he was an active duty soldier stationed at Fort Hood. Cameron James Wagenius, 22, was sentenced to prison on Friday, more than a year after pleading guilty to hacking telecommunication companies and extortion schemes tied to stolen data. According to the Justice Department, between April 2023 and December 2024, Wagenius was part of a group that conspired to hack and defraud at least 10 organizations. Using the online alias “kiberphant0m” as well as a hacking tool he helped to develop, and gained access to data from phone call logs. In November 2024, he sent two posts online that “disclosed stolen confidential non-content call detail records belonging to a government official and family members of another former official and threatened to release additional confidential records unless paid a ransom,” according to officials. The scheme targeted American and foreign telecommunications companies, with the plotters moving stolen information across the Telegram messaging app. The plotters, Wagenius among them, attempted to extort people for more than $1 million. They were able to sell some of the stolen data, according to officials. In the time between his arrest and plea he was kicked out of the Army. He had been serving as a private first class. Wagenius joined the Army in 2022 as a signal support systems specialist, Stars & Stripes previously reported .

title: Four airmen receive the Distinguished Flying Cross for Kabul evacuation actions
content: The crew of a C-17A cargo plane received Distinguished Flying Crosses this month for their actions during the U.S. evacuation of Afghanistan in 2021. Four airmen from the 758th Airlift Squadron, 911th Airlift Wing were presented with the award, given for heroism or extraordinary achievement during aerial flight on Sept. 12. The recipients are: Lt. Col. Eric Miller, 911th Operations Group pilot; Maj. Jason Mileham, 911th Operations Support Squadron operations chief; Master Sgt. Tyler Painter, operations superintendent; and Tech. Sgt. Steven Strobel, 758th Airlift Squadron loadmaster. Five years ago they took part in Operation Allies Refuge, where the U.S. military worked to ferry evacuees out of Afghanistan as the U.S.-backed government fell and the Taliban quickly seized control of the country. The Distinguished Flying Crosses were given specifically for their actions operating at Hamid Karzai International Airport, Kabul, Afghanistan on Aug. 27, 2021. It was a tense situation. A day prior, an Islamic State suicide bomber attacked one of the airport’s gates, killing 11 U.S. Marines, a Navy corpsman and an Army special operations soldier, alongside hundreds of Afghans. But flights continued and thousands were still at the airport, trying to get out of the country. The C-17A from the 911th Airlift Wing was one of the planes coming in to help with the evacuation. “Navigating an extremely hazardous night airspace under the threat of small arms fire and surface-to-air missiles, the crew reached the stricken airfield.

title: The Navy’s shipyard upgrades could take 50 years, cost $200 billion
content: The Navy’s plan to modernize and upgrade its four shipyards in the coming years could take half a century and cost more than $200 billion, a new report found. The Government Accountability Office released a new report on the Navy’s Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program (SIOP) on Friday. The report , “Naval Shipyards: Complete Information Needed for Decision-Making on Multibillion-Dollar, 50-Year Infrastructure Program,” found that the price tag has noticeably grown since it started, and that the effort lacks plans for regular reviews of its progress. That lack of oversight and evaluations risks further cost increases and new challenges. “However, the Navy has not outlined steps in the framework to reevaluate program objectives and resources as the program progresses over the next several decades,” the report said. “Without building such reviews into key future decision points, the Navy is limiting its ability to ensure that capabilities in SIOP’s plans today continue to be aligned or adjusted to support future fleet warfighting needs.” The Navy currently has four shipyards: Pearl Harbor in Hawaii; Norfolk, Virginia; Puget Sound, Washington; and Kittery, Maine. The shipyards are “essential” to maintaining operational readiness for the Navy’s ships, specifically its carriers and submarines, but they currently have outdated infrastructure and poor conditions, the GAO said. The overhaul program was started in 2018 and aims to give the shipyards new equipment as well as new or upgraded dry docks to better service the fleet.

title: Largest Army base in South Korea has no running water over holiday weekend
content: Soldiers at the Army’s primary base in South Korea have no running water and won’t have any through the weekend, service officials said on Friday. Officials said that a mechanical failure left taps dry across Camp Humphreys, 40 miles south of Seoul, but that fixes would be delayed through the weekend due to a Korean holiday. This weekend marks the three-day Chuseok harvest festival, which extends over Thursday, Friday and Saturday of this week. As a result of the holiday, officials said, U.S. troops, families and contractors on base could be without running water until Monday. A post on the base’s Facebook page said that several services were closed. “All [recreational] facilities, AAFES food services, AAFES Main Exchange, Zoeckler Mini Mall, Troop Mini Mall, Sentry Mini Mall, and 3rd MI Express are suspended,” the post said. “The 24-hour Family Mini Mall remains operational.” Dining facilities, officials said, remain open. The base gets approximately 70% of its water from the nearby city of Pyeongtaek, while the remaining 30% is sourced from wells on the base, according to previous reporting by Stars and Stripes . Base officials said nine “water buffalo” tanks were available around Camp Humphreys but that personnel would need to bring their own containers to fill. Army photo by Spc. Matthew Marcellus. Camp Humphreys is the largest overseas U.S. military installation, and home to the 2nd Infantry Division. The installation has an on-base population of about 45,000 service members , civilians, contractors, and their families.

title: UN report says drug boat strikes are war crimes. What does that mean for US troops?
content: U.S. troops carrying out strikes against alleged drug-trafficking boats are facing renewed questions about the legality of their orders after a United Nations expert found the attacks may constitute crimes against humanity . Ben Saul, the U.N. special rapporteur on counterterrorism and human rights, examined the U.S. military campaign that has killed 223 people in at least 68 strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific since September 2025. Saul found there were reasonable grounds to believe the U.S. strikes were murders under international law and that the campaign of killings could constitute crimes against humanity. He also rejected the argument that targeting alleged members of designated terrorist groups alone gives the United States a right to use military force in self-defense. The Trump administration has maintained that the strikes are lawful and that the United States is engaged in an armed conflict with drug-trafficking organizations the government has designated as terrorist groups. For those service members carrying out the strikes, the growing legal challenge could put them in a difficult position. In theory, military personnel could one day be held responsible for carrying out an order they know to be manifestly unlawful, under this week’s U.N. finding. But for individual service members, some likely to be junior in rank and used to following orders without hesitation, refusing an order the military considers lawful can bring immediate punishment and end a service member’s career.

title: Thunderbird’s 360-camera captured pilot’s safe ejection during crash
content: The Air Force Thunderbirds might be the most heavily photographed airplanes in the U.S. military. The Pentagon’s official photography archive lists over 20,000 photos and 500 videos of the team’s pilots and F-16 jets. But some of the most remarkable images ever released of the demonstration team were made public Monday inside the pages of a formal accident investigation report on the cause of a crash of one of the team’s jets last December . As the Thunderbird pilot ejected from that crash, less than 500 feet in the air, the plane’s canopy was jettisoned upward by small explosive charges. Attached to the canopy was a 360-degree video camera. As the canopy rocketed upward from the doomed jet, the camera kept filming. The images it captured are remarkable. In a span of just five seconds, the camera captured the pilot rocketing free of the jet from just a few dozen feet away. A second image, looking up through the clear canopy, shows the pilot’s parachute billowing open in midair. An image captured by an in-cockpit camera of a Thunderbird pilot under a parachute after ejecting on Dec. 5, 2025. The F-16 can be seen continuing to fly beneath the pilot. Air Force photo. A final image, just seconds later, captures the F-16 impacting the California desert in a massive fireball a few hundred feet below. The investigation that released the images found that a flaw in the jet’s engine was responsible for the crash, and cleared both the plane’s pilot and the unit’s maintenance crews of any culpability in the mishap.

title: 1st Infantry Division soldiers deploy to Lithuania in ongoing effort to deter Russia
content: Soldiers with the 2nd Brigade Combat Team, 1st Infantry Division, will deploy to Lithuania as the U.S. continues its military presence on NATO’s eastern flank, Maj. Montrell Russell, an Army spokesman, told Task & Purpose. They will be replacing the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 1st Armored Division, according to an August news release that previously announced the routine deployment. The deployment is part of Operation Atlantic Resolve and continues a U.S. presence that has regularly sent battalion-sized Army units to Lithuania since 2019. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the U.S. shifted to continuous rotational deployments in the country. Top Stories This Week News Fishing charter catches Air Force attack drone off Florida coast By Austin Campbell News Thunderbird’s 360-camera captured pilot’s safe ejection during crash By Matt White News 1st Infantry Division soldiers deploy to Lithuania in ongoing effort to deter Russia By Austin Campbell Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda announced Tuesday that the next U.S. rotation was already on its way. His office said the incoming force would be no smaller than the previous rotation, which included more than 1,000 troops, although Lithuania had not yet received an exact number from Washington. A U.S. European Command (EUCOM) official confirmed to Task & Purpose that Army units were continuing “routine deployments to Lithuania” under Operation Atlantic Resolve but did not confirm the number of troops deploying to the region cited by Lithuania’s president, citing operational security.

title: Top Army drill sergeant says basic training isn’t just about being tough: ‘We have to operate with empathy’
content: Sgt. 1st Class Kevin Harrington speaks with a clear, even voice, which, if you’ve ever met an Army drill sergeant, might be surprising. When he discusses life “on the trail,” as drill sergeants describe their jobs, his words are free of the raspy or strained tones that many in his profession have adopted after countless hours of shouted “corrections.” Part of his unblemished voice, he says, comes from good technique and the occasional cup of tea. “Tea with some honey sometimes,” he said. “And you have to not yell from your throat. You have to use that diaphragm if you need to be loud.” But mostly, he admits, he’s just, well, built for this. “I think I’m just naturally born loud,” Harrington said. “I have a louder voice. My wife swears I don’t listen when I talk, so I’m kind of a natural. When you have to make sure 240 individuals can hear you, because we get that many during our summer surges, we have to be loud to be heard, right?” Beyond his voice, as the 2026 Army Reserve Drill Sergeant of the Year , Harrington breaks most of the cliches associated with drill sergeants as a campaign-hatted disciplinarian. “You think of a ‘drill sergeant,’ you think of yelling, and this authoritative figure that’s always screaming,” Harrington told Task & Purpose. “But we’re so much more than that, right? We are coaches, mentors. We’re fathers. We’re chaplains. We have to operate with empathy.” (Left) Sgt. 1st Class Kevin Harrington, the Army Reserve drill sergeant of the year, and (right) Staff Sgt. Noel Berges, the active duty drill sergeant of the year during a Sept.

title: Pentagon identifies Virginia soldier as 19th death in support of Iran war
content: The Army released the identity on Tuesday of a soldier who died in the Middle East last week, a day after Task & Purpose confirmed the woman as the 19th U.S. service member to die while deployed in support of the Iran war . Capt. Bianca C. Wilkerson, 37, of Norfolk, Virginia, died on a non-combat flight to Saudi Arabia, the Army said, from a “medical incident.” Wilkerson was posthumously promoted to major, the Army said. Wilkerson was assigned to Headquarters, U.S. Army Central & Third Army, Shaw Air Force Base, South Carolina, and was deployed to Doha, Qatar, where she was “supporting overseas operations.” The Pentagon has been referring to the Iran war as “overseas operations” since July 7, when Department of Defense officials declared the end of Operation Epic Fury . The other troop deaths listed under Overseas Operations include four service members who died in July, three in Jordan and one in Iraq . Wilkerson’s death was added to the Defense Casualty Analysis System Sept. 21. Four other U.S. troops were listed under Overseas Operations, including four service members who died in July, three in Jordan and one in Iraq . “Since Operation Epic Fury has concluded, the Department classifies casualties as overseas operations in the [U.S. Central Command] area of responsibility,” a defense official said.

title: HII FF(X) Patrol Frigate Program Progressing as Navy Considers Foreign Options
content: Notional FF(X) frigate design. Navy image VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — Both U.S. and foreign designs for the next small-surface combatant are under consideration after the cancellation of the Constellation-class guided-missile frigate, the new head of the Navy’s shipbuilding enterprise said this week. A foreign design study is running in parallel with the development of HII Ingalls’ FF(X) Flight I patrol frigate, which was announced late last year following the Constellation cancellation, Portfolio Acquisition Executive Rear Adm. Casey Moton told an audience on Thursday at the American Society of Naval Engineers Fleet Maintenance and Modernization Symposium. Moton confirmed that the HII frigate had passed its critical design review (CDR) earlier this year, which had not been previously announced by the Navy, and was working with HII Ingalls Shipbuilding on the pre-production work. The Navy awarded a $282 million advanced contract for long-lead items in April . “We just went through CDR on the Flight I, and so we’re doing some pre-production activities with HII to help prepare for that material,” he said. PAE Maritime is also in the process of the mandated 90-day review of the foreign ship designs, working with “the other stakeholders within the Department of the Navy and [the Pentagon] and [the Office of Management and Budget] and others, talking about the various options, putting those together as part of the response to the presidential study,” Moton said.

title: Navy Establishes New Deputy Chief Of Naval Operations to Support Failing Shore Infrastructure
content: An aerial view shows construction progress on Dry Dock 5 (P-209) at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii, Aug. 7, 2026. Officer in Charge of Construction Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard leads construction of the new dry dock, a key component of the Navy’s Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program and the modernization of Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility. US Navy photo WASHINGTON NAVY YARD – Navy shore infrastructure will be in failing condition by 2037 if the sea service continues to use its current funding schedule, the new deputy chief of naval operations told USNI News on Thursday. As the newly created deputy chief of naval operations of sustainment, Vice Adm. Scott Gray, who will report on Oct. 5, will be tasked with continuously pushing for funding for shore infrastructure, including barracks and piers. “The idea is to continue the efforts to revitalize the shore, make wise investments and kind of bring the shore infrastructure back to where it needs to be to better support the needs of the fleet,” Gray said. Vice Adm. Scott Gray salutes as he arrives for a change of command ceremony for Commander, Navy Installations Command (CNIC) at the Washington Navy Yard, Sept. 24, 2026. US Navy photo On Thursday, fighting back a cold and some tears, Gray relinquished his role as commander of Navy Installation Command. The newly promoted Vice Adm. Brad Collins assumed CNIC in a change of command ceremony at the Naval History Museum.

title: Chinese Cutters, Warships Block Philippine Resupply Mission to Second Thomas Shoal
content: An undated photo of the Philippine Navy’s grounded World War II-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57). PLAN photo Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal on Thursday in the most significant development at the disputed South China Sea feature. The People’s Liberation Army Navy and China Coast Guard attempted to “hinder” the resupply mission, Manila’s National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea announced on Friday. “In doing so, they put Filipino personnel at risk and obstructed a legitimate humanitarian and sustainment operation,” reads the task force’s statement. Two Philippine Coast Guard patrol vessels, BRP Malabrigo (MRRV-4402) and BRP Cabra (MRRV-4409), were supporting the Philippine Navy-operated resupply ship Lapu Lapu when Chinese forces intercepted the resupply mission. According to a statement from the Philippine maritime security agency, the mission was temporarily suspended following “dangerous maneuvers” by the Chinese forces that threatened a collision with Lapu Lapu . The incident occurred 60 nautical miles away from Second Thomas Shoal. Vessel monitoring map dated Sept. 24, 2026. Philippine Coast Guard map A graphic released by the Philippine Coast Guard shows three Chinese cutters shadowing Cabra and Lapu Lapu . An additional force of 11 China Coast Guard and China Maritime Militia vessels were observed near the Philippine Navy’s grounded World War II-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57) at Second Thomas and Sabina Shoals.

title: ‘We Absolutely Need to Change,’ Says New Navy Maintenance Head
content: Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Industrial Operations, Rear Adm. Todd Weeks speaks with USS Bataan (LHD-5) crew members and staff at General Dynamics, NASSCO Shipyard in Norfolk, Va, during a visit to the Wasp-class multipurpose amphibious assault ship on Aug. 20, 2026. US Navy photo VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — Not quite two months on the job, a submariner turned head of the Navy’s vast maintenance operation promised his office would create a more nimble organization that would better balance risk to speed ships back to the fleet. Program Acquisition Executive for Industrial Operations Rear Adm. Todd Weeks told a crowd of ship maintainers the service wants to reduce the barriers to get ships out of maintenance on time. “We absolutely need to change, and we’re not getting it done. We just aren’t,” Weeks said Thursday while speaking at the American Society of Naval Engineers Fleet Maintenance and Modernization Symposium. “We’ve got to be better than we are and we [have] got to focus on what is it going to take to deliver the ship, the submarine, the aircraft carrier out of maintenance.” PAE IO is now in charge of the Navy’s major maintenance efforts including the 38,000 civilian maintainers across the four public shipyards and contracting with private repair yards for surface ship maintenance. The Navy’s public yards are largely responsible for fixing nuclear submarines and carriers while the surface Navy’s amphibious warships, cruisers and destroyers are maintained and modernized in a network of private yards across the country. Maintenance trends have not been positive.

title: Autonomous Aircraft Executes Mission Plan in Collaborative Tool Test, Navy Says
content: An MQ-20 Avenger surrogate aircraft demonstrates Collaborative Autonomy Mission Planning (CAMP) Sept. 10, 2026, during Gray Flag 2026, showing how human operator plans are seamlessly translated for autonomous flight execution. US Navy photo The U.S Navy recently demonstrated that an autonomous aircraft can receive a mission plan and execute that mission as part of the Collaborative Autonomy Mission Planning (CAMP) tool, the service announced Tuesday. CAMP is meant to integrate autonomous aircraft with mission planners, helping the two communicate in a common way. Mission planners develop the overall mission – including what each aircraft should do, when it should do it, and what authorities and limitations apply in the Collaborative Mission Planning Continuum (CMPC) – and then CAMP translates that information into a format an autonomous aircraft can use to carry out its assigned role as part of a larger battle plan, reads the Navy news release . “CAMP is about making autonomy more usable by integrating into mission environments with both manned and unmanned platforms,” said Capt. Todd “Toby” Keith, PMX-281 program manager. “This demonstration showed how we can connect the way operators plan missions today in the CMPC with the way autonomous aircraft will execute those missions. That can reduce the burden on our operators, improve interoperability and help bring collaborative autonomy closer to operational use.” The demonstration was carried out by a team from Naval Air Systems Command’s Strike Planning & Execution Systems (PMX-281) on Sept.

title: Report to Congress on Bahrain, Issues for U.S. Policy
content: The following is the Sept. 23, 2026, Congressional Research Service report, Bahrain: Issues for U.S. Policy. From the Report The Kingdom of Bahrain is a small island nation connected by a causeway to Saudi Arabia (15.5 miles away) and once claimed by Iran (124 miles away). Wedged between these two larger regional powers, Bahrain has hosted a U.S. naval command headquarters since 1948. For decades, Bahrain has permitted U.S. access to its facilities and has hosted U.S. Naval Central Command (NAVCENT) and the U.S. Fifth Fleet at a base called “Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain.” NSA Bahrain has long served as the logistical hub for U.S. maritime operations in NAVCENT’s area of responsibility and has hosted thousands of American soldiers, civilians, and their families. Since the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran began in February 2026, Bahrain’s security and economy have faced unprecedented challenges from Iranian retaliatory attacks against the island kingdom. To date, Iran’s drone and missile strikes have struck both Bahrain’s critical infrastructure and U.S. military facilities. As of fall 2026, numerous reports indicate that NSA Bahrain sustained serious damage in the opening days of the conflict. With NSA Bahrain damaged, U.S. Naval logistics operations have faced an array of challenges. Congress routinely reviews proposed U.S. arms sales to Bahrain, and Bahraini procurement of additional advanced protection systems to counter incoming missiles and drones from Iran may accelerate in the months and years ahead.

title: The Robot Ships of Route 90
content: NEW IBERIA, Louisiana – Surrounded by rows of sugar cane fields on Bayou Teche, generations of shipbuilders are wrenching on the U.S. Navy’s latest push toward a future drone fleet. Work boat builders and repair facilities dot U.S. Route 90 in southern Louisiana, where the boom and bust of the oil and gas industry looms over yards small and large. It’s along this road where several shipyards are vying for a chance to build unmanned ships for the world’s most powerful navy. At Breaux Brothers Enterprises outside of Lafayette, La., four aluminum Romulus vessels are currently under construction for a collaboration agreement between the yard and HII, the United States’ largest shipbuilder. Breaux Brothers has built high-speed vessels for the petroleum industry since the 1940s, when Brannon Breaux’s grandfather started building aluminum crew boats in Iberia Parish. “Undoubtedly, my family’s name – Breaux – has built more crew boats from the 40-something to 200-foot [range] than anybody else in the world,” Breaux, the president of Breaux Brothers and a third-generation boat builder, told USNI News over boudin and cracklins on a muggy morning visit in August. Breaux Brothers and yards like it in central Louisiana construct offshore support vessels, the pickup truck of the oil and gas industry. Yards built them by the hundreds during the height of the Gulf Coast oil and gas surge in the early 2010s and the glut of used boats served as the nucleus of the Pentagon’s early autonomous ship experiments.

title: 3 Years of Middle East Combat Altering How Navy Supplies, Maintains Fleet, Leaders Say
content: USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) departs following a replenishment-at-sea with fleet replenishment oiler USNS Henry J. Kaiser (T-AO-187) during Operation Epic Fury, March 18, 2026. US Navy photo This post has been updated to include that BAE Jacksonville received a $70 million maintenance availability for the Littoral Combat Ship USS Wichita (LCS-13). VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — The ongoing U.S. conflict with Iran is morphing how the Navy fixes and supplies ships operating thousands of miles from logistics hubs as extended time at sea and the prospect of an extended naval commitment in the Middle East are creating a maintenance wave back home, service officials said this week. As of Monday, there were more than a dozen guided-missile destroyers supporting carriers USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77) and USS George Washington (CVN-73) and the Boxer Amphibious Ready Group in the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, according to Monday’s USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker. USS Spruance (DDG-111) and USS McFaul (DDG-74) have been deployed since November – 10 months deployed. Combined with the expanded U.S. presence in the Red Sea in response to Houthi attacks in 2023, the Navy has been sailing ships into conflict for three years. “We are sustaining 15 warships in the [weapon engagement zone]. That’s almost four carrier strike groups’ worth of destroyers,” Capt. Eric Kellum, the chief of staff of Naval Surface Force Atlantic, said Wednesday during a panel at the American Society of Naval Engineers Fleet Maintenance and Modernization Symposium.

title: Taiwan Transfers Coast Guard Patrol Vessel to the Philippines
content: Ex-Kinmen (CG-123). Taiwan Coast Guard Administration photo MANILA, PHILIPPINES – An ex-Taiwan Coast Guard Administration patrol vessel is now under a Philippine flag in the most significant maritime security development between Taipei and Manila in recent years. The decommissioned Kinmen , one of four 500-ton Taipei-class patrol vessels commissioned between 2001 and 2008, appeared registered under the Philippines with the name BLING NO.1 on Sept. 16. Maritime tracking website VesselFinder placed the patrol vessel at the Southern Taiwanese port city of Kaohsiung, home to the bulk of Taipei’s Navy and Coast Guard vessels. The Coast Guard Administration of Taiwan clarified last week that the vessel transfer was based on the precedent of previous donations of retired patrol ships to partners such as the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu. Another statement from the maritime security agency on Sept. 20 said the transfer agreement stipulates that the former cutter “will never be used for law enforcement against Taiwanese fishing vessels.” This week, the West Philippine Sea (WPS) Foundation officially handed over the deed of ownership of the vessel to the Philippine Coast Guard in Manila. The Tuesday ceremony revealed that ex- Kinmen will be used for training purposes and missions around Mindanao, a Southern Philippine island located away from the South China Sea and Luzon Strait. All crew-served weaponry was removed before its transfer to Philippine service, according to media released by the WPS Foundation.
